claims.text: Compositionally complex alloys or high-entropy alloys can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Compositionally complex alloys and high-entropy alloys have inherent resistance to temper embrittlement.
Exposure over a range of temperatures can induce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in these alloys.
Conventional alloys undergo temper embrittlement within a characteristic temperature range.
High-entropy alloys have complex, multicomponent compositions.
The multicomponent composition hinders the formation of embrittling phases.
The alloy composition suppresses impurity segregation.
The alloy composition suppresses the formation of brittle phases.
Suppression of impurity segregation and brittle-phase formation maintains ductility across the relevant temperature range.
The alloy will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The transition will occur without the dramatic loss of ductility associated with temper embrittlement in conventional alloys.
The precise mechanisms by which compositionally complex alloys resist temper embrittlement are not fully understood.
Mechanical behavior in high-entropy alloys may vary with composition and processing history.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts maintained ductility across the temperature range, whereas the predicted ductile–brittle–ductile transition necessarily includes an intermediate brittle or substantially less-ductile regime.

Inherent resistance to temper embrittlement is presented as the reason for a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, but resistance to embrittlement does not itself explain how the intermediate brittle state would arise.
